templates.name: Callout
templates.summary: A one-page local trades site with services, hours, coverage checking, and emergency callouts.
templates.description:
Callout is a complete service-business website designed for an independent plumber, electrician, or other local tradesperson who needs to build trust quickly and turn nearby visitors into phone enquiries. The template gives a small operator the credibility of a larger company without introducing a complicated CMS or administrative workflow.

The customer journey is focused on practical questions people ask before booking: what the business repairs, whether emergency help is available tonight, which neighbourhoods are covered, and how to call. Service cards, opening hours, click-to-call actions, an interactive street checker, project photography, and a clear coverage map keep those answers visible throughout the page.

All business details, services, navigation, hours, and validation messages are centralized in typed constants for quick personalization. Original illustrations, responsive layouts, accessible form behavior, and carefully tuned mobile interactions make the template ready for vibecoding into a distinctive real-world trade website.

Four add-ons, a full service menu, transparent quote guidance, salon details, opening hours, click-to-call actions, and a four-question FAQ complete the path from browsing to booking.

templates.name: Today's Menu
templates.summary: A café and deli board that follows the clock — dayparts reorder by local time and sold-out dishes are greyed out.
templates.description:
Today's Menu is a one-page website for a café or deli whose offer changes through the day and who wants the website to behave like the board behind the counter. It is designed for owners who are tired of static PDF menus that say nothing about what is actually available right now, and who want visitors to see the current service — and what has already sold out — before they walk over or call.

The page opens with an editorial masthead and a live clock card that reads the visitor's local time: a status line such as "Serving lunch — until 4 pm", a sun marker moving along a breakfast–lunch–evening day strip, and a background band that warms from morning gold to evening amber. The three daypart menus reorder themselves so the current service always leads, with a tomato "Serving now" badge on the active sheet and "From 4 pm" or "Back tomorrow" chips on the others; before opening and after close the page shows honest kitchen-closed messaging. Dishes are set in classic dotted-leader typography with dietary tag chips, and sold-out items stay on the board struck through with a Sold out chip. An hours strip highlights today, a café story section, a click-to-call and email band, and a structured FAQ complete the page.

Everything an owner edits lives in two committed JSON files: site.json holds the name, contact details, weekly hours, and links, while menu.json holds the three daypart windows and every dish with its price, tags, and soldOut flag — flip one boolean to grey a dish out. The template ships as fully static Astro output with TypeScript content types, shared time utilities used by both the server render and the vanilla client scripts, plain hand-written CSS with tokens at the top of one stylesheet, FAQPage JSON-LD, accessible time labels and focus states, and layouts verified down to 320px.

templates.name: Bakery Preorder
templates.summary: A weekend baker's page with a live order cut-off countdown, collection slots that fill up, and email reservations for loaves and cakes.
templates.description:
Bakery Preorder is a single-page site for a weekend microbakery that sells small batches from a home kitchen and needs orders locked in before baking starts. It solves the two questions that decide whether a preorder lands: how long is left to order, and which collection slots still have space — answered by a live oven-timer countdown and a board of visibly filling slot tags.

The journey runs down one page: a hero introducing the bakery with the countdown to the configured Thursday 18:00 cut-off, this weekend's six bakes with photography and prices, four Saturday collection slots showing capacity meters with nearly-full and fully-booked states, and a reservation form with quantity steppers, a live order ticket, and a slot select that disables full slots. The countdown is computed from configuration, never a hardcoded date: it always targets the next occurrence of the cut-off weekday and time, and once this week's cut-off passes it rolls to next week and tells visitors that orders have reopened for the following collection date. Submitting the form composes a prefilled order email to the baker and confirms locally that nothing is sent until the visitor presses Send, with a copy-to-clipboard fallback — an honest pattern with no pretend server.

Personalization is two JSON files: src/data/site.json holds the bakery name, contact details, collection address, cut-off weekday and time, and bake day, while src/data/bakers.json holds the six bakes and four slots with capacity and reserved counts. The design is an original flour-and-blush direction with Yeseva One display type, an arched hero photo, tag-style slot cards, and a receipt-style order ticket, built as static Astro output with TypeScript content types, plain responsive CSS, accessible labelled controls, and FAQPage JSON-LD.

templates.name: Tap List
templates.summary: A live taproom keg board showing what's pouring, ABV, and how full every keg is — so regulars see what's about to blow before they visit.
templates.description:
Tap List is a single-page website for a taproom, brewery bar, or beer café whose real product changes nightly: the keg board. Printed menus and stale PDFs go out of date the moment a keg kicks, and regulars hate driving over for a beer that blew an hour ago. This template publishes the same board the staff keep behind the bar — eight numbered taps with beer name, brewery, style, ABV, pour size, price, and a vertical sight-glass gauge showing how full each keg actually is.

The board is the page. Each tap card pairs its specs and tasting note with a fill gauge that carries real states: fresh kegs get a brass "Fresh keg" chip, kegs under 20% turn to a pulsing "About to blow" warning with an amber-red gauge, and an empty keg is stamped "Blown" with a struck-through name and a drained, striped tube. Every gauge has an accessible text equivalent such as "about 63% remaining." A masthead status panel computed from the data counts pouring, about-to-blow, and blown kegs and shows when the board was last updated; filter chips narrow the board to hoppy, crisp, dark, or sour pours with a live "Showing X of 8 taps" count. Prominent click-to-call and email actions, address, opening hours, house rules for the board, and a five-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD turn board-watching into visits.

Everything a bar owner needs to change lives in two committed JSON files: src/data/taps.json holds the eight taps (name, brewery, style, family, ABV, price, pour, fill percentage, note) and src/data/site.json holds the business details, hours, and links — update a fill percentage and the gauge, warning states, and masthead counts all follow. The design is an original industrial taproom direction — deep green-black board, brass accents, chalk-white type, Bebas Neue and Space Grotesk — implemented in plain hand-written CSS with tokens at the top of one stylesheet. Built with Astro and TypeScript as a fully static site with vanilla-TypeScript interactivity, it lints and type-checks clean and stays responsive without horizontal overflow down to 320px-wide screens.

templates.name: Supper Club
templates.summary: A one-night pop-up dinner invitation with a live seats-remaining place card, countdown to doors, a menu revealed course by course, and RSVP by plain email.
templates.description:
Supper Club is a single-page invitation site for anyone hosting a one-night dinner: a pop-up, a private dining room, a chef's table in an apartment. These nights do not need a restaurant website or a ticketing platform — they need one elegant page that answers the four questions every guest has: when is it, how many seats are left, what will we eat, and how do I get a chair. Everything is driven by one committed event file, so the host edits a date, a seat count, and four courses instead of touching layout code.

The page reads like a candlelit invitation. Guests land on the club name, the dinner's theme, and a place-card counter showing seats remaining out of the cap — with a pulsing urgency state when the table is nearly full and an automatic waitlist mode when seats hit zero — above a countdown to doors that ticks live from the configured date. The tasting menu behaves the way it does at the table: four sealed course cards are uncovered one at a time, in strict order, by tap or keyboard, with an impatient-guest shortcut that reveals the whole card (and the full menu stays readable with JavaScript disabled). The RSVP form validates name, email, seats, and dietary notes, then composes a ready-to-send email to the host and says exactly what happened — nothing pretends a server received anything, and no seat is held until the host replies. If the date has passed, the page degrades gracefully into a join-the-list-for-the-next-dinner state. A five-question FAQ ships with FAQPage JSON-LD.

Personalization is two JSON files: site.json holds the club name, host, contact details, socials, and the venue-reveal policy; event.json holds the date (one ISO field drives the countdown, the displayed date, and the past-date fallback), price per seat, inclusions, seat cap, seats remaining, and the four courses with pairings. The design system — near-black aubergine, candle gold, ivory paper cards, Cormorant Garamond and Jost — lives in one hand-written CSS file with tokens at the top. Technically it is Astro static output with strict TypeScript, typed content models, vanilla-TS interactivity (no framework islands), ESLint, semantic HTML with labelled inputs and visible focus states, and layouts verified down to 320px-wide screens.

templates.name: Class Timetable
templates.summary: Weekly yoga and pilates timetable that highlights the next class with a live countdown and hands booking to your scheduling link.
templates.description:
Class Timetable is a single-page website for a yoga or pilates studio whose schedule repeats every week. Most studios run the same gentle rhythm — sunrise flows, lunch-hour sessions, candlelit evenings — yet publish it as a stale PDF or a screenshot on Instagram. This template treats the timetable itself as the product: the page opens with "Next class starts in" and a countdown ticking to the second, followed by the whole week laid out as one airy grid.

The next upcoming class is computed in the visitor's browser from recurring weekday-and-time rows, so it is correct at any moment with no hardcoded dates: after today's last class it rolls to tomorrow morning, and it looks ahead across the week when a day is empty. The highlighted card glows softly and carries a floating "next" pill with its own compact countdown, today's column is flagged, and a class that is currently running shows a pulsing "in session" chip with its end time. Booking is an honest handoff rather than a fake backend — when a scheduling link is set in the site data, the header button, the main call to action, and every one of the twelve class rows open it; when it is empty, the same buttons gracefully fall back to call and email links built from the contact details shown on the page. A five-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD answers the things people ask at the door.

Everything an owner edits lives in two committed JSON files: src/data/site.json for the studio name, address, phone, email, bookingUrl, socials, notes, and FAQ copy, and src/data/timetable.json for the classes — name, weekday, start time, duration, level, optional instructor, and a one-line focus. The schedule math sits in small typed utility modules, the design is a calm dawn-practice palette of sage, warm sand, and one terracotta accent set in Albert Sans with Lora italic accents, and the layout holds from a 1440px desktop grid down to stacked day groups at 320px, with reduced-motion support throughout. Astro ships it as fully static HTML with a single tiny script for the countdown.

templates.name: Quiet Practice
templates.summary: A calm counselling site whose gentle four-question self-check routes visitors to the matching service page — individual, couples, or teen counselling — every page static and shareable.
templates.description:
Quiet Practice is a multi-page website for a solo therapist or counsellor whose real problem is not looking pretty online — it is that prospective clients arrive anxious, skim a wall of text, and leave without knowing which service was meant for them. Instead of a long about page, the site leads with a gentle "is this right for me?" check: four small questions, one at a time in large serif type, that end by landing the visitor on the service page that fits what they described. The result is a real, shareable URL — not a generic contact form — and the check is honestly framed as a signpost, not a clinical assessment, with a disclaimer and an email fallback for people nothing quite fits.

The seed content ships three services — individual therapy, couples counselling, and teen counselling — each with its own statically generated page: an "it might fit if" list, how sessions would work, what the first session is like, and a sticky session-details card with length, fee, rhythm, format, and the booking action. Routing is a small typed utility: every answer adds weighted points to one or more services, the highest total wins, and ties resolve to whichever service led earliest — so "who would the sessions be for?" carries the most signal but consistent later answers can override it. Every service page also appears in normal navigation (homepage index rows, footer, cross-links), loads directly at its own URL, and a noscript note points no-JavaScript visitors to the plain service list. The homepage rounds out with a three-step "how it starts" strip, a four-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD, and a dusk-dark contact panel whose primary action is the configured booking link or a warm click-to-call fallback, with tel: and mailto: links always built from the same contact details shown on screen.

Everything a practice owner edits lives in three JSON files — site.json for names, credentials, phone, email, bookingUrl, hours, FAQs, and every section heading; services.json for the services, fees, and per-service accent tones; self-check.json for the questions and their routing weights — with scoring, contact-link, and currency-formatting logic kept in typed utilities. The design is a committed dusk-calm system: muted dusk blue, soft lavender, and warm grey on near-white paper, Source Serif 4 headings with IBM Plex Sans body, original abstract ripple SVG artwork instead of stock photography, and generous unhurried whitespace. Technically it is Nuxt 4 with Vue 3 and strict TypeScript, generated to fully static HTML (no server runtime) with all routes prerendered, ESLint flat config, vue-tsc type-checking in the build, reduced-motion support, visible focus states, semantic landmarks, and layouts verified down to 320 px wide.

templates.name: Couch to 5K
templates.summary: A nine-week running plan visitors tick off session by session, with progress saved on their own phone.
templates.description:
Couch to 5K is a single-page training-plan site for a running coach whose beginner clients keep losing the printed handout. The classic nine-week walk-run progression — twenty-seven sessions of roughly half an hour — lives on one fast page the runner keeps open on their phone. Every session card carries a coach-style title, exact interval instructions such as "Run 1 min / walk 90 sec — repeat × 8", and an approximate duration, and every week comes with a short note in the coach's voice.

The page is built around progress the runner can feel. Ticking a session saves it to localStorage on the device — no account, no sync, nothing uploaded — and the ticks survive reloads and revisits. Per-week counters, segment bars, a sticky header with week chips 1–9, an aria-live "12 of 27 sessions done" counter, and a slim progress strip all update the moment a box is ticked, and an original SVG trail map in the hero fills in coral from START toward the 5K finish flag as weeks are completed in order. A reset control with an explicit confirm step clears the device, mailto and tel actions route enquiries straight to the coach, and a five-question FAQ ships with FAQPage JSON-LD. Because the site is fully prerendered, it even renders sensibly with JavaScript disabled — checkboxes still tick natively, they simply don't persist.

Personalization is two JSON files: src/lib/data/site.json holds the coach, contact, and FAQ copy, and src/lib/data/plan.json holds all nine weeks, so a coach can rewrite the whole programme without touching a component. The localStorage store, session-id scheme, and progress wording live in small typed modules, styling is hand-written CSS driven by coral/navy/off-white design tokens with the Sora typeface, and the build is SvelteKit 2 with Svelte 5 runes and adapter-static producing a fully static build/ directory that passes ESLint and svelte-check and stays overflow-free down to 320 px.

templates.description:
Movement Library is a single-page website for a physiotherapy or physical-therapy practice that wants every patient to leave with a clear, repeatable home plan. Between appointments patients forget doses, lose handout sheets, and give up hunting through video links; this template puts the clinic's ten most-prescribed movements on one page, each written exactly the way it is coached in the treatment room — body-part tags, sets and reps or hold times, two-to-three numbered steps, and an honest caution note. No video hosting, patient accounts, or booking system is required, and a visible note states plainly that the library is general guidance, not a personalised prescription.

The patient journey is deliberately small: filter, add, print. Anatomical-tag filter chips for Neck, Shoulder, Back, Hip, Knee, and Ankle carry live exercise counts and update a "Showing X of 10 movements" status line. Every movement is a chart-style card pairing an original line-figure illustration with a kinesiology-tape dosage strip, numbered coaching steps, and a highlighted "Take care" warning. Add-to-plan buttons fill a plan tray that docks to the bottom of the viewport once it holds movements, with per-item remove, clear, and print actions — and the plan persists in localStorage, so it survives reloads and return visits. The centerpiece is the print flow: a dedicated print stylesheet hides the entire app and outputs only a clean black-and-white patient card with the practice name and date, a write-in "Prepared for" line, each movement's figure, dose, steps, and caution, Mon–Sun adherence tick boxes, and the practice contact line with the guidance disclaimer.

Everything a practice needs to change lives in two committed JSON files: src/data/site.json holds the practice name, physiotherapist, phone, email, address, hero copy, disclaimer, tray and print-card labels, and five FAQs (rendered as an accessible accordion with FAQPage JSON-LD), while src/data/exercises.json holds the movements themselves — edit a dose or add an exercise and the filters, counts, tray, and printed card all follow. Call and email actions are real tel: and mailto: links built from the same displayed data. The design is an original warm clinic-chart direction — paper white, ink navy, and kinesiology-tape green with Zilla Slab and Figtree type, chart-paper grid textures, and ten hand-drawn SVG stick figures sharing one visual grammar. Built with React 19, TypeScript, and Vite as a fully static SPA, it lints and type-checks clean, keeps controls keyboard-accessible with aria-pressed states, visible focus rings, and polite live regions, and stays free of horizontal overflow down to 320px-wide screens.

templates.name: Client Gallery
templates.summary: Private wedding photo delivery gallery where clients star favourites and export the list for their photographer.
templates.description:
Client Gallery is the delivery page a wedding or event photographer sends when the final selection is ready. Handing over finished photographs is easy; getting a useful answer back is not — the edit conversation usually stalls on "which ones do you want printed, retouched, or in the album?". This template turns that question into the page itself: a private, single-page gallery where the couple simply stars what they love, and the reply writes itself.

The album opens on a print-room masthead — the couple's names in Libre Caslon serif, the event date, venue, photograph count, and a quiet "Photographed by" credit — then flows into a charcoal masonry wall of twelve matted frames, each with a proof-sheet number, a caption, and its exact filename. Every frame carries a real star button with aria-pressed state; favourites persist per device in localStorage keyed by the album id, so choosing can span several evenings. A sticky tray keeps the running count visible ("7 of 12 favourited") and holds the two actions that matter: clear, and export. Export builds a CSV of the starred photographs — number, filename, caption, in album order — as a client-side Blob download the couple attaches to their reply. A four-question FAQ covering how favourites work, how to send the list back, and usage rights ships with FAQPage JSON-LD.

Every word and photograph on the page lives in one committed JSON file, src/data/album.json — swap the names, date, venue, credit line, captions, FAQ answers, and the twelve files in static/images/, and the gallery is yours. Design tokens (charcoal surfaces, ivory type, a single muted-gold accent, and both Google Fonts) sit at the top of one stylesheet. Under the hood it is a Gatsby 5 static build with React 18 and TypeScript: typed content models, favourites and CSV logic in small typed utilities, an ESLint flat config, semantic keyboard-accessible controls with visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and layouts verified down to a 320px viewport. There is no server, no accounts, and no environment variables — the build output is a folder of static files.

templates.name: Podcast Home
templates.summary: A show site with a real player — chapter markers on a waveform timeline and searchable transcripts — plus a directly loadable static page for every episode.
templates.description:
Podcast Home is a complete website for an independent podcast whose episodes deserve more than a bare embed. Podcast apps bury the back catalog and can't link to a moment, so when a listener is told "skip to the bit about tape ninety," they scrub blindly. This template gives the show its own home where every episode carries a real player with chapter markers and a transcript the listener can search, turning word-of-mouth recommendations into seconds-long lookups.

The home page skips the generic hero and opens on the latest episode ready to play: a waveform timeline with chapter pips, play/pause, a scrubbable playhead that also works from the keyboard, and a numbered chapter list — clicking any chapter or pip jumps the audio to that timestamp and starts playback, and the current chapter stays highlighted as the episode runs. Every episode gets its own statically generated page with the same player plus a searchable transcript excerpt that highlights every match, announces the match count, and scrolls the first hit into view; transcripts are server-rendered so they stay readable without JavaScript. Around the player sit an archive of every episode with original SVG cover art and mini waveforms, about and host sections, a five-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD, and mailto contact built from the same studio email shown on screen.

Everything a podcaster edits lives in two obvious places: content/site.json holds the show name, tagline, host bio, email, socials, and FAQ copy, while each episode is one markdown file whose frontmatter (title, number, date, duration, audio path, guest, chapters with start seconds) and dialogue-formatted body drive the whole site — add a file and the archive, routes, and navigation follow. Five short spoken demo clips ship in public/audio so the player, chapters, and timestamps work out of the box until real recordings replace them. The design is a bold audio-first identity — near-black base, rich violet, one acid-lime accent, Bricolage Grotesque display type with Schibsted Grotesk body — implemented as design tokens atop one global stylesheet with CSS Modules per component. Built with Next.js (App Router) and TypeScript using output: 'export', it ships a fully static out/ directory where every episode route loads directly on any static host, lints and type-checks clean, supports reduced motion and visible focus states, and stays responsive down to 320px-wide screens.

features.description: Every episode page carries a speaker-labeled transcript; searching highlights each match, announces the count via a live region, and scrolls the first hit into view. Transcripts are server-rendered and readable without JavaScript.

templates.name: First Chapter
templates.summary: Author site with a built-in reader for the whole first chapter and an honest buy-link handoff — no store to configure.
templates.description:
First Chapter is for a self-published author who needs one thing on launch day: a place where a stranger can fall into the book. Instead of a brochure page that points at retailers, the site carries the complete first chapter and lets visitors read it in the browser, in a real reader, before deciding to buy. There is no store, no checkout, and no signup to maintain — the site sells nothing itself and says so plainly, handing finished readers to whatever shop already stocks the book.

The landing view is set like a dust jacket: an original SVG/CSS clothbound cover drawn from the author's own title and imprint, a tagline, the blurb, praise quotes, an author bio with a working mailto link, and a five-question FAQ that also emits FAQPage JSON-LD. One click opens the reader view — a serif column of about 64 characters per line with a drop cap, epigraph, and scene-break ornaments, under a sticky chrome bar with a thin brass progress rule, live percent read, estimated minutes left, and A−/A+ text-size controls. Reading position and text size are saved to localStorage at paragraph level, so a reload — or a return visit days later — reopens the chapter exactly where the reader left off, and the landing hero switches to a "Continue chapter one" button with a percent-read chip. The chapter ends in a handoff card: buy the paperback at the configured shop URL, or write to the author.

Personalizing it is two files: replace src/content/book.md with your own opening chapter (plain Markdown; word count and reading time are recomputed automatically) and edit src/data/site.json for every visible string — title, author, blurb, praise, FAQ, buy URL and button copy, and even the reader chrome labels. The cover art redraws itself from the same data, so there is no cover image to produce. Technically it is a Svelte 5 + TypeScript single-page app built with Vite: Markdown is parsed into the bundle at build time with marked, reader logic lives in small typed modules, and the output is a fully static dist/ that any host can serve. Semantic HTML, keyboard-operable controls with visible focus, reduced-motion support, and layouts verified down to 320px wide are all in place.

useCases: let readers sample a full first chapter in the browser
send ready-to-buy readers to an existing bookshop page
launch a book without setting up a store
collect reader and book-club enquiries by email

templates.name: Drop
templates.summary: A countdown drop page for vintage one-of-one pieces that flip to a stamped SOLD state and are claimed by email.
templates.description:
Drop is a single-page shop for sellers whose stock is one of one — vintage jackets, worn-in boots, serviced watches, deadstock frames. Cart-based shop templates assume restocks and live inventory, which is exactly wrong for this kind of selling: each piece exists once, releases happen at an announced time, and the fastest email wins. Drop sells that ritual instead — a release the audience can watch approaching, pieces that visibly die when they are claimed, and rules stated plainly enough that nobody argues about who was first.

The masthead is a huge JetBrains Mono countdown ticking to the configured drop datetime, over an acid-orange marquee ticker that repeats the drop facts. Below it, eight pieces hang in a brutalist grid with era, size, condition, and price on every card. Before the drop, available pieces carry a "Drops Fri" chip and an "Ask about this piece" button that opens a pre-filled question email; the moment the datetime passes, the page flips in the browser to a giant LIVE NOW state — chips turn AVAILABLE and buttons become "Claim by email" with a CLAIM subject line, no redeploy needed. Sold pieces are unmistakably gone: greyscale photo, rotated SOLD stamp, struck-through price with a GONE flag, and no action at all. A three-step "How a drop works" section, an honesty strip explaining that SOLD stamps are updated by hand (no cart, no live stock counter), and a five-question FAQ with FAQPage JSON-LD round out the page.

Everything a seller edits lives in two committed JSON files: src/data/site.json (name, email, city, intro, steps, socials, FAQs) and src/data/drops.json (drop name and number, ISO datetime with timezone, and the eight items with sold flags). Countdown math, the upcoming/live state machine, date formatting, and the mailto builder are small typed modules in src/utils, and design tokens sit at the top of one CSS file. Technically it is React 19 in React Router framework mode with ssr disabled and the route prerendered, so npm run build emits plain static HTML that any static host can serve, hydrated only to run the clock. Semantic markup, a keyboard-accessible native-details FAQ, visible focus states, reduced-motion fallbacks, and layouts verified down to 320px wide come standard.

templates.name: Will It Survive?
templates.summary: Three honest questions about light, watering habits, and pets return the plants that will actually cope — with shareable link results and a tagged eight-plant bench.
templates.description:
Will It Survive? is a single-page site for a small plant shop that would rather sell one plant that lives than three that die. Most plant pages are aspirational catalogues; this one opens straight into a quiz about the buyer's real habits — how bright the flat honestly is, what their watering track record looks like, and whether anything in the house treats leaves as salad — and answers with the short list of plants the shop genuinely believes will survive there. The tone is the pitch: guidance from care tags, spelled out plainly, never dressed up as a live stock check.

Every answer is a real radio input inside a fieldset, presented as friendly icon cards, and every change is encoded into the page address (?light=low&care=forgetful&pets=yes) so results can be sent to a partner or flatmate; a shared link restores the same selections and the same verdict on load, and a copy-link button sits under the results. A complete set of answers returns two to four "survivors" as adoption-style cards with tag-derived reasoning lines like "Genuinely copes with low light" and "Forgives missed waterings". Combinations nothing fully fits never dead-end: the nearest plants appear flagged as close calls with the catch spelled out per plant, under a straight-talk note — and households with pets are never shown a non-pet-safe plant, not even as a fallback. Below the quiz, the whole bench is laid out as a tagged catalogue of eight plants with prices, personality one-liners, honest chips (including "Keep from pets"), and a "Reserve one" button that opens a pre-filled email built from the shop address shown on the page. A five-question FAQ ships with matching FAQPage JSON-LD, and the visit panel carries address and opening hours.

Personalizing needs no code spelunking: the shop identity, section copy, hours, reserve-email template, and FAQs live in src/data/site.json, the plants in src/data/plants.json, and every quiz label, reasoning line, and tag caption in src/data/quiz.json. The eight potted-plant illustrations are original inline SVGs keyed by plant id, with a fallback sprout so newly added plants render immediately. Under the hood it is Parcel 2 with vanilla TypeScript — no UI framework — with matching, reasoning, and URL-state logic in small pure typed functions, an ESLint flat config, design tokens at the top of one stylesheet, keyboard-operable controls with visible focus states, and layouts verified from 1440px down to a 320px viewport.

templates.name: Sunday League
templates.summary: An amateur football club noticeboard with the league table, fixtures, and the next match pinned and counting down to kick-off.
templates.description:
Sunday League is a club noticeboard for amateur football teams whose web presence is maintained by a volunteer secretary, not a developer. Grassroots clubs need one page that answers the questions people actually ask — where do we stand in the table, who do we play next, what time is kick-off, how do I join — without a CMS, logins, or a stats platform. Everything on the board comes from two committed JSON files the secretary edits after each final whistle, and the page says so honestly.

The board opens with a matchday poster that pins the next fixture: both club crests, home and away tags, the venue, the kick-off date, and a scoreboard-digit countdown ticking live to kick-off. The pinned match is computed from fixture kick-off times against the clock — nothing is hardcoded — so the poster rolls over to the following fixture on its own, and once every fixture has been played it degrades gracefully into a "Season complete — next season's fixtures soon" card. Below it sit a semantic HTML league table with the club's row highlighted and goal difference computed from the goals columns, a results list with won/drew/lost chips (including a "Result to follow" state for played games without a recorded score), upcoming fixtures with venues and times, an about-the-club strip, and a five-question FAQ that is also injected as schema.org FAQPage JSON-LD. Contact runs through mailto links built from the same secretary details displayed on the page.

Personalization is two files: src/data/club.json holds the club name, ground, colours note, secretary contact, about copy, and FAQs, while src/data/season.json holds the table rows and fixtures — the README documents every field, including how results are recorded from the club's point of view. The design is original club-noticeboard art direction: pitch greens, chalk white, one gold-trophy accent, Oswald scoreboard type with Inter body copy, six hand-drawn geometric SVG crests, and a chalked centre circle behind the poster. Technically it is Angular 22 with standalone components, signals and zoneless change detection driving the one-second clock, strict TypeScript over typed JSON imports, ESLint flat config with angular-eslint, keyboard-accessible controls with visible focus states, reduced-motion support, and layouts verified down to 320px where the table scrolls inside its panel rather than the page.

templates.name: Route Library
templates.summary: A club route book with distance and climb filters, SVG elevation profiles, and a GPX download for every route.
templates.description:
Route Library is a route book for a running or cycling club whose best routes usually live in long-standing members' heads, a dusty forum thread, or a drawer of printed maps. It turns that knowledge into a public, filterable library: every route has a measured distance, an honest climb figure, a surface and grade, a named start point, a written description and a downloadable GPX file, all presented under the club's own name and contact details. The seeded content is a fictional Lake District fell running club with five internally consistent routes, so the shape of a finished site is visible before a single edit.

The home page opens straight into the book: a filter bar for distance (under 10 km, 10–25 km, over 25 km) and climb (under 300 m, 300–700 m, over 700 m) above a grid of route cards, each carrying a mini elevation sparkline and stat blocks. Filtering is done on the server through query parameters, so every filtered view is a shareable URL that works without JavaScript, while a small enhancement script makes the same filters instant in the browser and keeps the URL in sync with history.pushState. Each route's server-rendered page at /routes/<slug> draws a full inline SVG elevation profile from the committed data points — area wash, axes, gridlines, a labelled high point and a hover crosshair with tooltip — backed by an accessible data table, a GPX download served with the correct application/gpx+xml content type and attachment header, a run-at-your-own-judgment note, and links to the rest of the book. Unknown slugs get a proper 404 page, no-match filters get an empty state with a mailto fallback, and a five-question FAQ ships with FAQPage JSON-LD in the layout.

Everything a club would change lives in two JSON files: src/data/site.json for the club name, meet point, club-run times, librarian contact, disclaimer and FAQ copy, and src/data/routes.json for the routes themselves, with matching GPX files in public/gpx. Filtering, formatting and the SVG chart geometry are typed TypeScript modules in src/utils, so the data stays plain and the logic stays out of the templates. Technically it is a compact Express 5 server with EJS views and no client framework: TypeScript compiled by tsc to dist/, tsx for the dev loop, ESLint flat config, semantic keyboard-friendly HTML with visible focus states, an original topographic design system (cream paper, contour linework, one burnt-orange accent, Chivo and Spline Sans Mono), and layouts verified down to 320 px.

templates.name: Registry
templates.summary: A device-local gift list with clear availability, private claiming, and optional shopping links.
templates.description:
Registry is a focused gift-list template for weddings, housewarmings, baby showers, and other occasions where guests need a simple way to choose a present. It helps non-technical hosts publish an attractive list while being explicit that claims are stored only on each visitor's device rather than synchronized by a backend.

Guests browse twelve categorized gifts, follow optional shopping links, claim an available item, and release their own claim when plans change. Availability counts update live, seeded examples demonstrate the claimed state, accessible disclosures answer common questions, and repeated device-only messaging prevents the interface from implying account-based reservation.

Gift details and editable page copy are centralized in committed content files, while colors, typography, motifs, and responsive behavior are separated into clear style modules. Vue 3, TypeScript, Vite, localStorage persistence, semantic controls, and static output make the project straightforward to personalize and deploy without services or environment variables.

templates.name: Reception Seating Plan
templates.summary: A drag-and-drop event seating planner with shareable URL state and a clean print view.
templates.description:
Reception Seating Plan is a one-screen planning tool for wedding and event organisers assigning guests to tables. It replaces paper sketches and fragile spreadsheets with a visual workspace that remains practical on desktop, mobile, and keyboard-only workflows.

Organisers can drag guests onto seats, select a guest and activate a seat, move assignments, return people to the manifest, or clear the arrangement. Every valid assignment is reflected in compact URL state for sharing and direct restoration, while live seat counts and dedicated print styles produce a clean plan without editing controls.

Guest names, table definitions, interface copy, geometry, and visual tokens live in clearly named TypeScript and CSS files. Svelte 5 and Vite provide a small static build, with typed state, accessible alternatives to drag and drop, responsive layouts, and print-specific presentation ready for venue-specific personalization.

templates.summary: A transparent rent calculator that prices unequal rooms by size, windows, and en-suite access.
templates.description:
Split the Rent is a practical calculator for flatmates who want a defensible alternative to dividing monthly rent equally when bedrooms differ. It turns room size, window quality, and en-suite access into visible weighted scores so everyone can discuss the same assumptions instead of arguing over unexplained totals.

Users enter total rent and configure between two and six rooms with names, floor areas, window choices, and en-suite toggles. A live fairness receipt explains base shares, adjustments, weighted results, and largest-remainder rounding, while URL-backed state lets the complete scenario be copied and reopened without accounts or stored data.

Editable labels, demo values, currencies, and weighting rules are separated into focused constants files, with calculations and URL parsing kept in typed utility modules. React 19, TypeScript, Vite, accessible form controls, hand-written responsive CSS, and exact-to-the-penny output provide a strong base for adapting the tool to another currency or fairness model.

templates.name: Overlap

templates.description:

Users search a keyboard-friendly catalog of 22 cities, add or remove locations, and adjust a shared working-hours window. The board shows local hours, UTC offsets, daypart colors, current-time markers, exact common ranges, or the closest fallback hour, and the full setup can be restored from a copied URL.

Nuxt 3, Vue 3, Vite-powered static generation, native Intl formatting, local fonts, accessible controls, and responsive strips make the template easy to rebrand or extend with additional cities without requiring an external timezone API.

templates.name: Launch

templates.name: Compare

It gives buyers and evaluators a structured shortlist covering concrete criteria, pricing context, best-fit guidance, and explicit product limitations.

Visitors begin with a decision brief, scan four products across ten criteria, inspect marked strengths and competitor wins, and review a candid where-we-lose row. Astro 6, TypeScript, semantic table markup, keyboard-focusable mobile scrolling, structured WebPage, SoftwareApplication, and FAQ data, plus responsive CSS tokens make the comparison easy to keep specific, current, and visually distinct.
